pulls.title: fuzz: torcontrol: drive the control connection over a mocked socket
pulls.body:
The `torcontrol` fuzz target hands made-up replies straight to the `TorController` callbacks, and caps reply lines at 16 characters. As a result, most success paths can't be reached, and the code that parses the control port (`ProcessBuffer()`, `ReceiveAndProcess()`) never runs.

This rewrites the target around a fake Tor on the other end of a real `TorControlConnection`, connected through `DynSock`. Replies go over the wire. The fake Tor answers each command the controller sends with a reply of the matching shape, so inputs can complete the whole handshake: PROTOCOLINFO, authentication (including SAFECOOKIE), GETINFO and ADD_ONION. The harness also checks that reply data never splits a command or injects a new one.

The first commit fixes `DynSock::Wait()`, which deleted its own socket. The bug has been there since #30205; this target is the first caller.

### Testing

Line coverage of `src/torcontrol.cpp` goes from 52% on master to 81% after a 10-minute local run. The master number is from the qa-assets corpus. Most of what remains is the controller thread itself, which the harness replaces, and socket errors that `DynSock` can't produce.

The input format changes, so the corpus in qa-assets needs a refresh.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Skip legacy wallet records rather than erasing them, and drop unused record erase functions
pulls.body: When migrating a legacy wallet, we can skip the records in `MigrateToSQLite` that we would delete later on during migration. These records are specifically all of the legacy wallet records, and transaction records. The legacy wallet records are replaced with descriptor records produced during migration, and transaction records are already being rewritten by migration, so not writing them in the first place is also fine. This allows us to remove several database record erase functions, specifically EraseTx and EraseRecords.

pulls.title: wallet: make migration more robust against failures
pulls.body:
This is just me finding a few more edge cases after #34156 and #34176

The goal of the PR is to handle failures in a controlled way. Just so the process can automatically restore the original wallet without requiring user manual intervention.

The covered cases are:

1. During `DoMigration()`: There are methods that can throw exceptions and abruptly abort the process. 
Instead of crashing (GUI) or returning a generic exception, we now will catch and return the error gracefully. This lets the process restore the original wallet automatically.

2. Trying to migrate a wallet in a read-only directory throws a filesystem exception and skips cleanup.
 Now the process will fail gracefully with a clear error msg, and automatically restore the original wallet.

3. Any failure during `MigrateToSQLite` requires user manual intervention. 
Now the original wallet db will remain untouched, and only be updated once the sqlite db creation fully succeeds.

pulls.title: wallet: fix migration with watch-only transactions
pulls.body:
Fixes #36483

As described in the linked issue, migration to descriptor wallets currently fails for legacy wallets that contain no spendable keys and are tracking watch-only transactions.

When a database transaction containing `RemoveTxs()` is aborted, the database rolls back and the registered `on_abort` callback is invoked. The current listener contains an empty `std::function` so calling it throws `std::bad_function_call` and masks the actual migration error.

The first commit changes the callback to a no-op function since no memory cleanup happens on abort. It also adds a unit test to confirm that abort restores the database record and leaves wallet memory unchanged.

After this commit, the [functional test](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36483) supplied by the issue's author changes from `bad_function_call` to `Error: Not all transaction records were migrated (-4)`, exposing the migration error previously masked by the abort callback exception.

During wallet migration, `RemoveTxs()` defers deletion of transactions from the original wallet's in-memory `mapWallet` until after the database commit. The current check that requires an empty map before the database commit causes migration to fail.

The second commit moves the check for an empty `mapWallet` to after `RunWithinTxn()` commits the database transaction and runs the commit callback, when transactions marked for removal have been deleted.

A new functional test is added to cover migration of a blank wallet with watch-only transactions. It checks that the destination watch-only wallet retains both transactions and balance, including after unloading and reloading the wallet, without rescanning the blockchain.

pulls.title: wallet, migration: Contain all legacy wallet and migration related things in its own subdirectory, namespace, and classes
pulls.body:
Originally, legacy wallet migration was built upon the foundation of being able to load legacy wallets. Now that we no longer support loading legacy wallets, there is no reason to keep any of the legacy wallet loading and migration code in the main wallet objects. Having this co-mingling of never-to-be-changed legacy wallet code and new descriptor wallet code makes it difficult to implement new things into the wallet.

This PR fully separates out all of the legacy wallet related things into a subdirectory `wallet/legacy`, with everything in that directory under a `wallet::legacy_migration` namespace so as to prevent accidental usage outside of legacy wallets. This includes a little bit of duplication with current loading code, but not that much, and we are able to both remove unrelated descriptor wallet loading from the legacy wallet loading, and unrelated legacy wallet loading from normal descriptor wallet loading.

`LegacyWallet` is introduced as a subclass of `CWallet` which contains all of the relevant legacy wallet and migration functions so that `CWallet` cannot accidentally use some legacy wallet function. Additionally, `LegacyDataSPKM` is moved into a new file and this new namespace so that it cannot be used outside of migration.

Lastly, `ReorderTransactions` is a legacy wallet only function that is also moved into `LegacyWallet`.

Builds upon #34909, and depends on #36823 for removing some functions that were previously used by migration.

pulls.title: rpc: Return the right RPCErrorCode more consistently
pulls.body:
Currently, rpc code may return the wrong `RPCErrorCode`. This is perfectly fine, because they should be hit rarely in production.

However, it could be good to be self-consistent. (Otherwise, we could just remove the different error codes and return a single one)

So fix a few error codes:

* An integral out-of-range is now `RPC_TYPE_ERROR`, not `RPC_MISC_ERROR`
* Some invalid args are now `RPC_INVALID_PARAMETER`
* Some transient issues or user-config issues are now `RPC_MISC_ERROR`

Follow up suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36791#discussion_r4568050151.

`waitNext` measures its timeout and 1-second fee tick with the wall clock, while `waitTipChanged` uses the steady clock. This means a wall clock jump changes how long `waitNext` waits, and it never times out while mocktime is frozen.

pulls.title: wallet: Clear streams before advancing BDB cursor
pulls.body:
This fixes a case where migratewallet can reject an old wallet as corrupt, i.e. this occurs on wallets used in Bitcoin Knots. The v2 key metadata may include an extra flag byte that Core’s metadata loader leaves unread. 

LoadRecords reuses its key and value streams between records. BerkeleyROCursor::Next() appends to those streams, so unread bytes from one record become part of the next and can cause a deserialization error.

Clear both streams before copying the next record, matching SQLiteCursor::Next(). This keeps the existing metadata parsing and migration code.

The regression test reads two records while leaving part of the first key and value unread, then checks that the second record replaces both outputs.

Testing on Linux:
- Without the fix, the regression fails both stream-content checks.
- With the fix, test_bitcoin --run_test=db_tests passes all tests

pulls.title: p2p: Use separate compact block nonce per network
pulls.body:
This issue was reported by ajtowns on IRC some time ago.

For compact blocks, when we serve the last compact block from cache, we use a single nonce for all peers currently.
This means anyone can request the most recent tip as a compact block via `getdata(MSG_CMPCT_BLOCK)` over a clearnet and a tor connection and then compare the nonces - if they match it's the same node.

Fix this by using a different nonce per network/bind (`CNode::m_network_key`). 
This means a little bit more work in `NewPoWValidBlock` where we will now create `CBlockHeaderAndShortTxIDs` objects for each network on which a peer has made us their hb peer. More instances may be created later when serving non-hb peers via `GETDATA`. Note that while on master, the `CBlockHeaderAndShortTxIDs` was created eagerly, and its serialization lazily, we now create both objects lazily.

From a high-level point of view, there are various remaining fingerprinting vectors even with this fix, some hard to fix, but I do think that we should be fixing at least the most obvious ones.

pulls.title: Implement BIP 54 (Consensus Cleanup) without mainnet activation
pulls.body:
This implements the Consensus Cleanup validation rules proposed in [BIP 54](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0054.md). These rules are only enabled on regtest. Mainnet activation, if any, is to be considered separately.

This patchset is based on the code that was previously reviewed ([1](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/99), [2](https://github.com/bitcoin-inquisition/bitcoin/pull/110)) and tested (for instance [here](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/consensus-cleanup-demo-of-slow-blocks-on-signet/2367)) on Bitcoin Inquisition. The tests and documentation have since been improved, but the consensus-critical commits have been carried over with only minor differences (the only behavioural one being the addition of the stripped-size check to `PreChecks`).

Roughly 95% of the added lines are tests or test data. The format, contents, and reproduction procedure for the BIP 54 test vectors are documented [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/tree/master/bip-0054/test_vectors). The `bip54_tests` unit test module exercises each mitigation extensively in isolation. The `feature_bip54.py` functional test verifies all of them end-to-end after and prior to activation. For the timestamp rules, it simulates timewarp and Murch–Zawy attacks, demonstrating the new timestamp rules prevent these exploits. A fuzz harness for the sigop accounting logic is also included, which can be seeded from the BIP test vectors (implemented [here](https://github.com/darosior/bitcoin/tree/bip54_seed_fuzz_corpus)).

See commit messages for details.

Currently there is no test coverage for oversized CompactSize. This is fine, because a vector this large will already be rejected earlier by the P2P transport payload size check.

However, it would be good to still add test coverage:

* Removing the check would pass all tests.
* There is some accidental non-deterministic coverage through tx-deser "fuzzing", which hurts coverage reports, see https://github.com/corecheck/corecheck/pull/219#discussion_r4554170963.
* Having explicit end-to-end P2P coverage for such corrupt messages seems fine.

pulls.title: txindex: allow running in pruned mode
pulls.body:
After #35531, each txindex entry now points to the block hash containing the tx instead of the file location of the block. The block hash is then used to find the file position of the block to read the tx from. This allows us to determine the hash of the containing block even if the block is later pruned, and also determine the location of the block on disk if it is later downloaded again via `getblockfrompeer`.

This PR enables maintaining a txindex while pruned. If a txid lookup tries to read a tx from a pruned block, the hash of the missing block is surfaced to the caller.

If desired, a user may call `getblockfrompeer` using the returned hash to download the block, then try again successfully. The downloaded block will be added to the front of the block queue, so won't be pruned again for at least 288 blocks. Of course a larger prune setting is desired if lots of historical blocks will be read, and there are privacy issues if the user is looking up their own transactions. Ideally the blocks can be fetched from a trusted node or from random peers with decoy blocks fetched occasionally.

Resolves https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/10609, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/12651, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/16182, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/35240

pulls.title: kernel: let callers create the block manager
pulls.body:
The kernel creates its block storage inside `btck_chainstate_manager_create`, configures it through the chainstate manager's options and reads blocks through the chainstate manager. Pruning (#35627) needs block storage that the caller can configure, keep and prune directly.

This adds `btck_BlockManagerOptions` and `btck_BlockManager`. `btck_chainstate_manager_create` takes a block manager and keeps a shared reference to it, so either handle can be destroyed first. A block manager can be passed to only one chainstate manager, and a failed creation still uses it up unless the contexts differ. `btck_block_read` and `btck_block_spent_outputs_read` take the block manager, and block tree entries are valid for its lifetime, which can be longer than the chainstate manager's.

Changes for callers:
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_create` no longer takes a blocks directory.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_wipe_dbs` is replaced by `btck_block_manager_options_update_wipe_block_tree_db` and `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_wipe_chainstate_db`. The block tree db is wiped when the block manager is created, and wiping it also wipes the chainstate db, which the old function required anyway.
- `btck_chainstate_manager_options_update_block_tree_db_in_memory` moves to the block manager options.
- Both options objects take the same total database cache, and each uses its own share.

Based on #36739. Draft until it is merged. Feedback on the API is welcome in the meantime.

pulls.title: kernel: add manual pruning
pulls.body:
Part of #35627 and kernel-node/kernel-node#111. The kernel can't open a data directory that a pruned node created, and it has no way to prune.

This adds a prune option on the block manager, `btck_block_manager_prune_up_to_height` and `btck_chainstate_manager_flush`. With the option set, the kernel opens pruned data directories. The chainstate manager created with the block manager decides what may be deleted, so pruning fails without one.

Pruning writes only block storage, never the chainstate. After an unclean shutdown the chainstate on disk is at the last flush, and recovering from there needs the blocks above it. Pruning therefore keeps every block above the fork point between the last flushed block and the active chain, and reports `btck_PruneStatus_NEEDS_FLUSH` when that bound limited what it could delete. The caller can flush and prune again.

The fork point matters when the flushed block was reorged out. Recovery then disconnects the stale blocks, which needs their block and undo data, and connects the new ones from their block data. `btck_block_manager_prune_reorg_tests` covers that case and fails if the bound uses the flushed block's height instead.

A fast prune option lets tests prune, since test chains never fill a 128 MiB block file.

Based on #36738 and #36854. Draft until both are merged.

pulls.title: net: only monitor select exceptions while connecting
pulls.body:
Alternative approach to #36688, citing the relevant parts of its description:

> There is currently nothing preventing us to receive TCP urgent data, which would never be returned by `recv()`. Linux's `poll()` is indifferent to this, but the `select()` socket monitoring may keep reporting it as pending on some platforms.
>
> This would not prevent progress nor lead to a crash anymore after #36665, but it's still undesirable.

Fix this by only adding a socket to the `select()` exception set while waiting for a non-blocking `connect()` to complete. Windows needs that to detect a failed connection. Established connections no longer monitor the exception set on any platform. This approach was suggested by theuni in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36716#issuecomment-6931290348 and replaces the earlier version of this PR, which ignored the exception set outside Windows and disconnected on it on Windows.

We could instead have set `SO_OOBINLINE` on our sockets, so `recv()` returns any urgent data sent to us (and likely leads us to disconnect the peer). RFC 6093 doesn't forbid this, but the current approach seems more clear and direct to me.

The PR makes one additional change for clarity: if `errorSet` is reported for a socket we did not request to read from, disconnect directly instead of first attempting a send that would fail (emits a different log message). `if (recvSet || errorSet)` is left as is. Since `select()` no longer reports errors for established connections, this only applies to `poll()`.

A new unit test in `sock_tests` covers the fix itself: with an urgent byte pending, waiting for `RecvEvent` must time out. Without the fix it fails on a `select()` build.

`p2p_socket_errors.py` checks that the node ignores a single urgent byte: the connection stays open, ordinary data is still processed and the urgent byte is not counted as received. It also covers a peer reset while the node is sending, for the `poll()` change above.

Backports until 29.x are straight-forward, but for 31.x and before require compensating for the scripted-diff in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/f395acdeeeaa1f3fd75d3cedbf2731fa24083e9f, for the log format change in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/22335474d768f99067856173ff2764b6db753f67. If we also want to backport to 29.x then the scripted diff for https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/fa9cf38ab666b50b0d8e82cb17f9e5a8a613547d and the infamous https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/9f36962b07eff2369577a17c8adeaa0433697e1c need to adjusted for.

pulls.title: refactor: break the blockstorage/validation circular dependency
pulls.body:
`node/blockstorage.cpp` includes `validation.h`, and the lint lists `node/blockstorage -> validation -> node/blockstorage` as an expected circular dependency. This removes it, and the lint confirms the cycle is gone.

The largest user of validation in block storage is `ImportBlocks`, which drives validation. It moves to `node/chainstate` and sets the reindex flag through the new `BlockManager::SetBlockfilesIndexed()`, which writes the flag to the block tree database and sets the in-memory flag under one `cs_main` hold. The last commit moves `FatalError` to `kernel/fatal_error.h`, after which `blockstorage.cpp` no longer includes `validation.h`. `validation.h` still exports `FatalError` for its other users.

Validation also reaches into `BlockManager`'s private members as a friend. `RequestPrune()` and `MarkBlockIndexDirty()` replace the friend declarations, keeping `m_check_for_pruning` and `m_dirty_blockindex` non-public. Both require `cs_main`, and the annotations let the compiler check it. After this, nothing outside `BlockManager` writes its private state or the block tree database.

There is no behavior change to my knowledge.

Based on #36738. Draft until it is merged.

Thanks to musaHaruna, who [suggested `RequestPrune()`](https://github.com/pzafonte/bitcoin/pull/2#discussion_r4283138022) in his review on my fork. The flag marks a pending pruning check, so callers request it and storage decides whether anything qualifies, which keeps the flag private once the friend declarations are gone.

pulls.title: refactor: Use CBlockIndex parameters as reference
pulls.body:
This is a janitorial refactor, a continuation of #34440. Input method parameters of type `const CBlockIndex*` are changed to reference `const CBlockIndex&` in some places where it makes no sense to call with a nullptr.

Motivation: slight improvement in code quality, maintainability and robustness.
- more explicit representation of the non-null input invariant
- less chance of nullptr-access error with future code changes
- more explicit checks at call sites for the non-null input invariant.

The following methods are affected:
- `LastCommonAncestor()` in chain.h
- `PeerManagerImpl::FindNextBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `PeerManagerImpl::TryDownloadingHistoricalBlocks()` (net_processing.cpp)
- `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterRange()`, `BlockFilterIndex::LookupFilterHashRange()` (blockfilterindex.h), and `LookupRange()` in blockfilterindex.cpp
- `BaseIndex::ProcessBlock()` (base.h)

General guidelines:
- When a method has an input of type `const CBlockIndex*`, and by contract it cannot be nullptr, change it to `const CBlockIndex&`. The reference type is an implicit documentation of the nun-nullptr invariant.
- When calling a method with reference parameter, ensure that it cannot be nullptr (it is often derived from a pointer), by/because:
  - explicit prior check and error handling
  - an assert/Assert/Assume
  - itself being a non-nullptr invariant input
  - it is being an output from a method with no-nullptr output invariant
- For local variables, use reference types whenever possible, for non-nullptr references
- For technical reasons pointers are still used even in some non-nullptr cases:
  - containers/variables that can staty unitialized initially
  - containers that need `reserve()`
  - using reference type in `std::set` would result in some copy constructor calls
  - `std::optional` cannot hold a reference type

pulls.title: Configuration argument handling improvements.
pulls.body:
Several numeric configuration options now reject values that are out of range instead of silently wrapping or inverting. Previously a negative value could disable the intended limit entirely.

  - `-dbbatchsize` and `-dbcrashratio` must be non-negative. A negative `-dbbatchsize` wrapped to a huge value and disabled batch flushing, so a reindex could hold an unbounded batch in memory.
  - `-limitclustersize`, `-limitancestorcount`, `-limitdescendantcount`, `-mempoolexpiry`, `-datacarriersize`, `-maxsendbuffer`, `-maxreceivebuffer`, `-bantime`, `-bytespersigop` and `-maxtipage` must be non-negative.
  - `-limitclustercount` must be between 1 and 64.
  - `-timeout` must be positive. It previously fell back to the default silently, unlike the analogous `-peertimeout`, which already errored.

  Zero remains valid wherever it already meant "disabled": `-dbbatchsize=0`,
  `-limitclustersize=0`, `-datacarriersize=0`, `-mempoolexpiry=0`,
  `-maxtipage=0`, `-bytespersigop=0`, `-maxsendbuffer=0`,
  `-maxreceivebuffer=0` and `-bantime=0`.

- The `-help` output for `-bytespersigop`, `-datacarriersize`, `-dbbatchsize`, `-stopatheight` and `-checkblockindex` now shows the `=<n>` placeholder for their value, matching how they are actually parsed.

pulls.title: validation: Ensure Invalid ValidationState has result
pulls.body:
Block and transaction validation results are represented in `ValidationState`, and invalid results in "Invalid" states. Invalid validation results have a `result`, an enum value, and a `reject_reason`, a structured string.

The change is to ensure that an __invalid result always has a set result and reject reason__. This increases code robustness/security.

One instance was identified where the result was not set, and is being fixed by a new `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result. PR #31981 moved a previous-block check from outside of `TestBlockValidity()` to inside it, and introduced a new usage of `BlockValidationState` with unset result. The result field is not checked outside. This instance is changed now to use the newly-introduced `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` value.

The new enum value is added to the kernel C API and its C++ wrapper. In P2P, a `BLOCK_INCONCLUSIVE` result does not lead to punishing the peer.

A few test-only instances with empty reject reason are changed to use a dummy value ("dummy-reason").

History: this was found on the side of #35570, but left untouched there; see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#issuecomment-5739477357 and https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35570#discussion_r4075379069.

pulls.title: net: stop using a socket once a wait reports an error
pulls.body:
ConnMan and the HTTP server would still try to read (and send) when a wait reports ErrorEvent. This means they could still read even when a read was not requested.

On select() based platform (BSDs, macOS and Windows), ErrorEvent can be returned if a peer sends us urgent data (we register the exception set because of a Windows quirk). However we can't read that urgent data, and this means we could be continuously woken up.

There is a number of things we could do to improve the situation here (see discussions in #36761), but in the meantime fix this bug by simply disconnecting immediately upon error. For consistency, adopt the same behaviour across all callers.

This PR is an alternative to #36716.

pulls.title: init: Fix surprising behaviors of negated options
pulls.body:
While looking into #36759 I discovered `-notorcontrol` did the opposite of what would be expected from it and I then checked for similar issues in other init options. There are several more where `-nofoo` does something surprising including one of them crashing the node.

This PR attempts to fix all these surprising behaviors while also keeping things as simple as possible and just change behavior to something that makes sense harmless in the context of the option. Fixes that use a common approach for the fix are grouped together into a commit even if the options included themselves may have no relation at all.

| Commit | Problematic options behavior | Fix approach |
|---|---|---|
| [mempool: Reject cluster limits below 1](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/512773d111daaa4330c873ed5889b9ef511f6e3a) | `-nolimitclustercount` hits an assertion in `TxGraph` on the first mempool transaction. `-nolimitclustersize` rejects every transaction. | Reject values below 1 at startup. |

The `-no*notify` options run the command `0`, `-nosigner` uses `0` as signer, `-noi2psam` fails startup and `-norpcpassword` sets the password to `0`. Opt-in because options like `-noonion` and `-noblockfilterindex` depend on reading `"0"`. | New opt-in flag `NEGATE_TO_EMPTY` makes `GetArg()` return `""`. |
| [init: Read -cjdnsreachable and -help as booleans](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/dc4ddbacf791ac6742261bf66dcf42887bfb74ff) | `-cjdnsreachable=0` and `-nocjdnsreachable` turn CJDNS on. `-nohelp` prints the help. | Use `GetBoolArg()` instead of `IsArgSet()`. |
| [args, wallet: Fix empty and negated -blocksdir and -walletdir](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/be71581c2fc65722f6e335e6506cda342eb23ef7) | `-noblocksdir` writes block files relative to the working directory. `-nowalletdir` fails startup. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. An empty value falls back to the default directory, like `-datadir` does. |
| [init: Require -nolistenonion with -notorcontrol](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/44b1c5b05057bf3a768eac63922c085163975dcc) | `-notorcontrol` connects to `0.0.0.0:9051`, which reaches a local Tor. | Fail at startup unless `-listenonion` is disabled. |
| [init: Disallow negating options where it has no meaning](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/commit/6447b07919072f12aba36313814fd4962dd4363a) | `-nocheckblocks`, `-nomaxreceivebuffer`, `-nomaxsendbuffer` and `-nomaxtipage` read as 0, the opposite of what the user asked for. | Fail at startup with `DISALLOW_NEGATION`. |

pulls.title: net: reimplement private broadcast as jobs isolated from the node
pulls.body:
Split out of #36608, the overall private broadcast rework to support ease of review for like-for-like feature.

Differences from #36608 :
1. No tool support or prep refactors for the tool
2. No package relay
3. Slimmed down test profile focusing on protecting aginst IP address linkage and not crashing the node on adversarial inputs (which is a leak in itself)

With `-privatebroadcast`, `sendrawtransaction` queues a job instead of handing the transaction to
the connection manager. Each job runs on its own thread, shares no state with the node, and
reaches the network only through the Tor proxy: it resolves the chain's DNS seeds, then announces
over BIP324 to recipients on a schedule drawn up front, each connection with fresh isolation
credentials. Nothing a recipient does, and nothing the node sees of the transaction coming back,
changes the plan, and the transaction enters the node's mempool only when it returns from the
network. The old private broadcast connections and relay are removed.

The invariants are specified in `doc/design/private-broadcast.md`.

The rest of the tests are in a follow-up to be considered later:
https://github.com/instagibbs/bitcoin/tree/2026-10-pb_reimpl_followup

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: Add analyzedescriptor for multisig setups
pulls.body:
Part of the multisig setup work tracked in #35645. Based on #35918 (the first 3 commits).

Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.

This PR adds that check in three layers:

1. **Inspection** (commits by w0xlt, with small changes listed below): `GetKeyInfo()`, `GetKeyInventory()` and `GetPolicy()` describe a parsed descriptor's key expressions, where each key is used, and how they combine. `getdescriptorinfo` gains a `verbose` option that returns them as `keys` and `policy`.
2. **Multisig analysis, no wallet:** `AnalyzeDescriptor()` tells whether a descriptor is a recognized k-of-n setup, and if not, why. `getdescriptorinfo verbose` returns it as `analysis`, so it works even with `-disablewallet`.
3. **Wallet part:** `interfaces::Wallet::analyzeDescriptor` (for the GUI) and the `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC add which keys the wallet holds, whether it can sign, and the first receive address. They accept any descriptor, single-sig included; `analysis.recognized` tells whether it is a safe k-of-n.

Recognized setups are `wsh(multi)`/`wsh(sortedmulti)`, and `tr(K,multi_a)`/`tr(K,sortedmulti_a)` with a single leaf, where `K` is the BIP 341 NUMS point or a `musig()` of at least k distinct cosigners. Every cosigner must be an extended key with an unhardened ranged derivation, and no two cosigners may be the same key. Anything else is still analyzed and returned, with `recognized: false` and the list of issues: the analysis warns, it never refuses a descriptor.

Example, run by one of the three cosigners:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=alice analyzedescriptor "wsh(sortedmulti(2,[a1b2c3d4/48h/1h/0h/2h]tpub.../<0;1>/*,...))"
{
  "keys": [
    { "role": "ecdsa", "type": "bip32", "xpub": "tpub...", "derivation": "/0/*",
      "origin": { "master_fingerprint": "a1b2c3d4", "path": "m/48h/1h/0h/2h" }, "wallet": "mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" }
  ],
  "analysis": { "recognized": true, "shape": "wsh_multi", "sorted": true, "threshold": 2, "cosigners": [0, 1, 2], "issues": [] },
  "can_sign": true,
  "first_address": "bcrt1q..."
}
```

A **locked wallet** is not an error: a cosigner key with a hardened origin path can't be checked without the private key, so it is reported as `"unknown"`, and `can_sign` is left out unless another key is already known to be the wallet's. Everything else (`analysis`, `first_address`) is still returned, and the caller can ask the user to unlock and retry. Only the candidate private key is decrypted.

#### Commits

| | Commit | Author |
|---|---|---|
| 1‑3 | #35918 | pseudoramdom |
| 4‑7 | key/policy inspection, `getdescriptorinfo verbose` | w0xlt (see changes below) |
| 8 | `script: add AnalyzeDescriptor() for multisig setups` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 9 | `rpc: add multisig analysis to getdescriptorinfo verbose` | |
| 10 | `wallet: add analyzeDescriptor to the wallet interface` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 11 | `rpc: move descriptor key and analysis JSON helpers to a shared file` | move-only |
| 12 | `wallet, rpc: add analyzedescriptor` | co-authored with w0xlt |


#### Changes made to the inspection commits (4-7)

The inspection commits come from w0xlt's descriptor inspection [branch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...w0xlt:bitcoin:feature/descriptor-key-inspection-simplified). These changes were made on top, for w0xlt to review and agree with or not (this section will be removed once agreed):

- *script: expose key expression structure* (was "expose structured key program data")
  - Use `m_root_extkey` instead of `*GetRootExtPubKey()`.
  - The derivation test also covers `/0h/*` and `/1/*h`, checking the last-hardened and derived caches.
  - `wide += ')'` instead of `")"` in the participant test (clang-tidy `performance-prefer-single-char-overloads`).
- *script: identify descriptor key occurrences*
  - `KeyRole()` is pure virtual; descriptors without key arguments (`addr`, `raw`, `sh`, `wsh`) say so explicitly with `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE()`.
  - Comment noting that `frame` is invalidated by the following `push_back`.
  - The walletload test mock is reduced to `return {}`.
- *script: expose descriptor policy nodes*
  - The header documents the two forms of the same construct (descriptor function vs Miniscript fragment).
  - `Assert` → `CHECK_NONFATAL`; explicit `static_cast<uint32_t>` for the threshold.
  - The fuzz target checks where each child role may appear (tap leaves only under `tr`, `script` only under `sh`/`wsh`, the Taproot internal key only on `tr`, the output key only on `rawtr`).
- *rpc: add verbose option to getdescriptorinfo*
  - The multipath note moved to the `verbose` argument help; the `policy` help explains both forms.
  - Tests for an origin without a path and for MuSig participant origins.

Open question: `script/descriptor_analysis.h` describes and gives no verdict, while `script/descriptor_analyzer.h` gives the verdict; the names are easy to mix up. Rename the first to `script/descriptor_inspection.h`?

#### Design choices

- An unrecognized descriptor claims no setup: no threshold, cosigners, sorting or key path. For example `wsh(sortedmulti(2,A,A,C))` is not a 2-of-3, since A alone can spend. Each issue lists the key IDs involved instead.
- The same xpub with different paths in two cosigner slots is a `repeated_key`, as is an xpub and its own child xpub. BIP 388 allows the same key with disjoint paths in general policies, but in a k-of-n it lets one holder fill two slots.
- A Taproot key path is either `nums` or `musig`. Any other internal key, a `musig()` of fewer than k cosigners, or one with an outsider or a repeated cosigner is `key_path_spendable`.
- For a multipath descriptor every path is analyzed and must be the same setup (`branches_differ` otherwise). `keys` and `policy` describe the first path.
- `can_sign` means the wallet holds the private key for at least one key of the descriptor, whatever its shape. Whether it is a safe k-of-n is a separate answer, `analysis.recognized`.

The functional test scenarios of #36325 were adapted here. The analysis differs from that wizard in a few places:

- `wsh(multi(...))` is recognized, with `sorted: false`: it is a valid k-of-n, and requiring `sortedmulti` was the wizard's own policy.
- A `musig()` key path of at least k distinct cosigners is recognized: those cosigners can already spend through the leaf.
- A single-path descriptor (`/0/*`) is recognized; `multipath_expansion` already shows whether it is multipath.

#### Known limits

- A cosigner key is matched against the wallet's HD keys exactly, or by deriving its origin path from the HD key with that fingerprint (normally the master key). If the wallet only holds an imported account xprv, keys below it are matched only exactly.

A release note will follow.

pulls.title: net: check network activity in ThreadOpenConnections
pulls.body:
Seednodes are used for addr-fetch connections. When the network is disabled (`networkactive=0` or `setnetworkactive false`), the seednodes are consumed without ever being dialled and  When the network becomes active again, no further addr-fetch attempts are made, even though the seednodes are still configured. They remain unavailable until the node is restarted.

This happens because `ThreadOpenConnections()`, continues running its loop while the network is disabled. With < 2 outbound peers or an empty addrman, a seednode is popped from `seed_nodes` , queued as an addr-fetch, and then popped again from `m_addr_fetches` in `ProcessAddrFetch()`. It is then dropped because `OpenNetworkConnection()` returns early when the network is inactive. Once the network is re-enabled, no seednodes remain. Anchors were lost in the same way before #34213.


This change makes `ThreadOpenConnections` wait while the network is re-enabled, as the way `ThreadPrivateBroadcast` does, so no connection state is used up while the network is disabled

wallet: Require the descriptors flag when the FLAGS record is missing
pulls.body:
`LoadWalletFlags` checks for `WALLET_FLAG_DESCRIPTORS` only inside `if (batch.Read(DBKeys::FLAGS, flags))`. A SQLite wallet file without a FLAGS record is loaded with no flags set and then handled as a legacy wallet, which ends in an `Assert`:

- with a legacy record in the file: `SetupLegacyDataSPKM`, `Assert(m_database->Format() == "bdb_ro" || m_database->Format() == "sqlite-mock")`
- without one: `LoadActiveScriptPubKeyMan`, `Assert(IsWalletFlagSet(WALLET_FLAG_DESCRIPTORS))`

`loadwallet` on such a file aborts the node. If the wallet is in the load on startup list, the node aborts on every start. The existing check for legacy records in a descriptor wallet (`UNEXPECTED_LEGACY_ENTRY`) does not catch this, because it also depends on the flag.

The second commit does the check whether or not the record exists, so the file is rejected with the legacy wallet error.

The first commit is needed for that: `bitcoin-wallet create` opened the new, empty database through `PopulateWalletFromDB` before it wrote the flags, which is the case the comment "The FLAGS key is absent during wallet creation" refers to. `CWallet::CreateNew` does not load anymore, and now the tool does not either. It writes the version records itself, as `CreateNew` does.

**Behavior change:** a wallet database without a FLAGS record no longer loads. `bitcoin-wallet create` writes the same set of records as before (compared by record type on a new wallet).

**Measurement:** regtest, RelWithDebInfo, base a527a0077a, descriptor wallet made with `createwallet`, then edited with sqlite3.

| file | master | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FLAGS record deleted | node aborts, `wallet.cpp:3577` | error -4, node keeps running |
| FLAGS record deleted, `cscript` record added | node aborts, `wallet.cpp:3404` | error -4, node keeps running |
| unchanged | loads | loads |

**Tests:** new case in `wallet_descriptor.py` for both files; on master the node aborts in it. Three unit tests that load a hand written database now write the flags first. Passing locally: `test_bitcoin` and `test_runner.py` with the default list. Not run: fuzz targets, lint.

pulls.title: Keep witness stacks in serialized form in CScriptWitness
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521. This PR focuses on reducing memory usage of transactions in memory, leaving performance improvements for other PRs.

`CScriptWitness` stores a witness stack as a `std::vector<std::vector<unsigned char>>`, which costs a 24-byte vector object and an allocation for every non-empty element. This makes it possible to construct transactions that take a large amount of memory after deserialization.

This PR first introduces encapsulation for `CScriptWitness`, hiding its representation. The last commit then changes the representation to be single `std::unique_ptr<byte[]>` which for non-empty witness stacks stores their serialization prefixed by a small length header. Witnesses can no longer be modified in place; they can only be replaced in their entirety. Access to the individual witness stack elements is done by on-the-fly deserialization instead.

`CScriptWitness` shrinks from 24 to 8 bytes, and `CTxIn` from 112 to 96 bytes. Worst-case allocated size for transactions kept in memory drops from roughly 28 bytes/WU to 1.6 bytes/WU.

This worsens deserialization and validation time, adding some 50-70 ms per block to the worst case for me. A follow-up #36918 with optimizations improves the worst case deserialization time significantly instead. Other minor degradations:
* libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
* `CScriptWitness::back()` is $\mathcal{O}(n)$ in the length of the witness stack.

Issue reported by furszy and 0xB10C.

pulls.title: Reimplement private broadcast as node state-less jobs + package relay support
pulls.body:
## Goals

Goal 1: Remove reliance on, and probes about, internal node state from private broadcast

Goal 2: Specify observable behavior to aid reimplementation and reduce profile fingerprints across versions

### Layout

Four parts, each starting with an empty marker commit:

1. support: moves shared code into the common library; no behavior change
2. bitcoin-privbcast: the specification and the standalone tool
3. bitcoind -privatebroadcast as jobs: the node runs the tool's job; the old relay and connections are removed
4. package mode: one parent and its child. Its validation commits (saturating fee sum, test-accept as submission, self-paying parent) serve only this part.

For the v33 release, I think 1 through 3 should be the goal, but the roadmap could be trimmed down to remove tool-only code if the conceptual support for the standalone tool is not there.

The tool itself introduces about 600 loc of logic, and also necessitates some of the prep move-only commits putting things in common. The vast majority is the shared Job machinery.


## Node-less state

The primary failure mode of the in-master private broadcast is that it relies on node state for operation, and this has led to a number of "careful coding" fixes:

1. The v2->v1 retry connected directly, without the proxy: #35319 (merged in #35410)
2. Discouraging a misbehaving peer gave a clearnet oracle: #36312
3. Eager job completion via mempool inspection: #36277
4. Private broadcast connections wrote to addrman: #35032

There are many other sources of fingerprints as well, some harder than others to exploit, and to fix. The solution: remove reliance on node state entirely to drive attempts. The spec states the goals as:

- A job reveals neither the sender's IP address, onion address nor node identity to any party.
- A hostile recipient, DNS seed or Tor exit learns no more than an honest one. It can only affect delivery.

### Jobs, slots and opportunities

- **Job**: one broadcast of one transaction, from submission to its report. A job spends its first 12 s finding candidates (IPv4/IPv6 addresses from the DNS seeds, resolved through Tor exits), then delivers. It runs for at most 10 min.
- **Slot**: one of a job's 6 independent delivery targets. Each slot tries to announce the transaction to one peer and serve it when asked. Slots 0–2 open when delivery starts; slot 3 opens 35–180 s later; slots 4–5 open 185–240 s later, at least 5 s apart. Each of these times is drawn at random within its range.
- **Opportunity**: one of a slot's 4 scheduled connection times: a first attempt and up to 3 fallbacks, each 50–60 s after the previous. A fallback runs only if the slot's previous attempt failed before announcing; once a slot announces, its remaining opportunities are dropped.

The times are drawn at job start, and each opportunity's candidate is fixed when discovery ends, before any peer is contacted. Nothing a peer does moves them (C1–C4). A job makes at most 24 connections, at most 6 of them at once.

### Differences at a glance

| | master | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Where it runs | Inside `bitcoind` only | `bitcoind -privatebroadcast`, or the standalone `bitcoin-privbcast` with no node; the same job either way (U3), with a JSON report of every connection |
| Recipients | `addrman.Select()` over onion, I2P, and IPv4/IPv6 through the proxy; networks follow `-onlynet` | DNS seed names resolved through Tor exits (RESOLVE), IPv4/IPv6 only; no node state used (R1, R6) |
| Connections | `CConnman` peers of type `PRIVATE_BROADCAST`, visible in `getpeerinfo` | The job's own proxy streams, each with fresh SOCKS credentials, so each gets its own circuit; not peers of the node |
| Plan | 3 connections, then more whenever the tx is stale (5 min, then 1 min) until it comes back from the network | 6 slots of 4 opportunities, all scheduled at job start; no retries; at most 10 min |
| Transport | v2 when addrman advertises it, otherwise v1, with a v2→v1 retry | BIP324 v2 only, with one constant VERSION per release (B4, E1) |
| Node settings | Shape which networks and peers are used | Peer-selection settings don't apply to jobs (U2) |
| Packages | — | `submitpackage` with one parent and one child: announce the child, serve the parent on request |

### No addrman

Under master, the node's private broadcast destinations are drawn from the node's addrman. Other parties write to that table through addr gossip, which makes it a unique fingerprint vector, and inherently attacker influenced. This rules out drawing recipients from anything the node or its peers can write to.

Its replacement is querying DNS seeds in a predetermined way under a static profile. This is inherently less robust than the p2p network in terms of liveness, but leaves no fingerprint within a release. The marginal fingerprint is the set of DNS seeds per release, which affects who is queried and exactly how. Each RESOLVE returns one address and exits cache answers, so each seed is asked through several exits: 4 Tor circuits, each querying all 7 seeds, for up to 28 results, which are assigned to the 6x4 opportunities before any dialing happens. A circuit per query, 28 in all, kept Tor busy enough that overlapping discoveries lost answers.

If the list shrinks, grows, or is modified, the release is revealed to the Tor exits carrying the queries, which see every seed name queried. A DNS seed learns only that it is on the list, and only when the exit has no cached answer.

The fingerprint potential also precludes fixed seeds, which change greatly each release, and which degrade in connectivity over time regardless.

### Minimal release fingerprint

Once a release is cut, behavior profiles are intended to be identical per user. This precludes user knobs and per-instance parameters, and requires a constant user agent and VERSION.

Across releases, the reimplemented p2p message state machine allows better control of unnecessary profile breaks going forward.

### Specification

`doc/design/private-broadcast-tool.md` comes before any code in part 2. It has goals, a threat model per party (recipient, exit, seed, network observer, guard), 54 numbered invariants (A–U, N), parameters, interface, assumptions, non-goals and a rationale. Code comments and tests cite the invariant IDs, so review can check code against a stated property. Concept review of the goals, threat model and non-goals is most useful first, then review of the implementation against the invariants.

This implementation is actually the second implementation, initially implemented solely via the spec and black box tests, which were handed to an otherwise blind agent.

### Tradeoffs

- Needs Tor, including Tor's RESOLVE extension. I2P is gone, and so are onion recipients. To re-add these, we need a connect->GETADDR step, and then have to filter out most of the addresses that do not answer when dialed.
- DNS seeds and Tor exits learn that a job ran, in addition to end recipients.
- No retries beyond the scheduled fallbacks. Retrying would act on whether the transaction comes back, which the adversary controls; the user resubmits instead.
- `getprivatebroadcastinfo` now reports jobs, and the connections no longer show in `getpeerinfo`.

pulls.title: mining: handle negative and NaN wait timeouts
pulls.body:
An ipc client can pass any timeout to `waitTipChanged`, but the code assumes it is never negative:

```
Assume(timeout >= 0ms); // No internal callers should use a negative timeout
```

On debug builds, a negative or NaN timeout fails this check and aborts the node. I reproduced this with a timeout of -1.0.

On release builds the check is skipped. Negative values are clamped to zero, but NaN is not, because every comparison with NaN is false. It ends up as the deadline passed to `wait_until`.

`waitNext` has no Assume, but it also doesn't check its timeout. A NaN timeout waits one extra fee tick (about one second) before returning.

We now treat negative and NaN timeouts as zero in both methods, removes the Assume, and documents the behavior in the interface. The functional test covers negative and NaN timeouts for both methods.

I'm not aware of any client that sends these values (sv2-tp, for example, requires an interval of at least one second), so this is hardening against bad input from ipc clients.

_This is similar to #36520, which handles invalid arguments to the Chain interface for the same reason._

Links

- https://ipcbugs.ofsky.org/bugs/bitcoin-2026-wait-timeout-assume/

pulls.title: Detect transaction problems early during deserialization
pulls.body:
This is split off from #36521 (and not included in #36895), as it's effectively an independent improvement.

This introduces a number of additional checks that are applied during transaction deserialization, which reduce various worst case deserialization time scenarios:
* Reject transactions with more txins or more txouts than can possibly fit in a block (applied always)
* Reject transactions with 0 txins or 0 txouts (applied in P2P code only; there are RPCs like `fundrawtransaction` that explicitly support transactions with 0 inputs)

This is a mild behavior change, as detecting these problems early causes them to be treated as deserialization errors, which in P2P logic cause messages to be ignored instead of peer disconnection.

pulls.title: rpc: generateblock to allow multiple outputs with custom payouts
pulls.body:
## Generatetomany

First approach was to create a `generatetomany` rpc call. That approach can be seen here https://github.com/polespinasa/bitcoin/pull/3

## Generateblock
Modifies `generateblock` to allow a user to set multiple outputs in the coinbase transaction. If an empty set is provided, the block will be empty. If no set of transactions is provided, the block will mine the mempool. If a set of transactions is provided only that set of txs will be mined.

```
$./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock bcrt1qw6qkj8wtw5hraxwxjp08m4aymkntms3yhqyacj
{
  "hash": "7359a3ed7af0f18f4016e6cb29193bd787a2452c584781135c585d5204b9ec5b"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]'
{
  "hash": "6db028454b26d6667dd6df45be2772844121fb44f86433f6bbfbafa429974684"
}

$ ./bitcoin-cli -rpcport=18443 generateblock '["bcrt1qal6p633hvwz2yp5mav0qy7u2az8gkn2xywnj6v", "bcrt1qvr3qgyhw6y0e0zj97v0j5yc40xtpea4wqj0g43"]' []

{
  "hash": "33e2ddc52546ddb0edf28bef5b295ee8fbd487b8aca19c97018467e2477877df"
}

```

### Motivation
https://x.com/SuperTestnet/status/1921220086645342550

Citating @supertestnet 
> When mining a block on regtest, the command "generatetoaddress" is available if you want to send the entire coinbase to 1 address. Let's add generatetomany in case you want to split up the coinbase among multiple addresses, similar to how the "sendtoaddress" and "sendmany" commands both exist and let you send money to (1) one address or (2) multiple addresses. The generatetomany command would be particularly useful for simulating protocols that send money to multiple recipients directly from a coinbase, as several pools do now, like ocean and braidpool.

pulls.title: net: make address overlap impossible when relaying addresses
pulls.body:
`CService::GetKey()` didn't include the network in the output. So in theory it would be possible for two IP2 and Tor addresses to have the same output from `CService::GetKey()`.

This would have unexpected results when used in the per-peer bloom filter of known addresses - we may wrongfully assume that a peer knows `foo.onion` when we have sent to them `foo.i2p`.

To make this impossible - include the network in `CService::GetKey()`.

Addrman already includes the network separately so it does not need this change. The code would be simplest if addrman also uses `GetKey()` with the network but that would mess the positions of addresses in existent databases (`peers.dat`). So, keep a variant of network-less `GetKey()` for addrman.

pulls.title: kernel: add btck_witness_stack_get_items
pulls.body:
With the change on #36895 : 
> libbitcoinkernel's witness stack element accessor becomes O(n) in the index of the witness element; using it to iterate a whole witness may therefore become O(n^2).

This adds `btck_witness_stack_get_items` which reads the stack in one O(n) pass and writes each item's pointer and size into two arrays passed to it. `WitnessStackApi::GetItems` is the C++ wrapper. The pointers are valid as long as the witness stack exists.

An earlier version passed each item to a callback from the bottom of the stack to the top. That order followed the serialization, which can only be read from the bottom up, more than how a stack should actually be read. This version lets the items be read from either end.

pulls.title: test: avoid BSD ephemeral-port collisions in HTTP clients
pulls.body:
While stress-testing #36147 I noticed sporadic port collisions still occurring on FreeBSD.

`set_ephemeral_port_range()` keeps the source port out of the test port range, but only for sockets the framework creates itself. Python's `http.client` creates its sockets internally, so RPC and REST connections can still be given a source port inside the test range. A connection to a closed port can then connect to itself. For example, the wrong-RPC-port startup check failed with `BadStatusLine: POST / HTTP/1.1` because the client read back its own request.

This change adds a `netutil.HTTPConnection` subclass that sets the port range before connecting, and uses it in `AuthServiceProxy` and in the tests that open HTTP connections directly.

HTTPS is left unchanged because we don't serve RPC over TLS so it seems unnecessary.

pulls.title: test: SRD tie-break test
pulls.body:
I was researching coin selection when I came across this bug, so I thought I'd fix it

Pr #33223  adjusts  weight selection to keep the lighter coin when two coins have the same value, but the test has two mistakes, as confirmed in this [comment ](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36255#discussion_r4432516127)

1. It builds `mixed_weight_pool` but passes `utxo_pool` to `TestSRDSuccess`.
2. There is nothing enforcing coin eviction because the current max weight (`4 * 3 * 67` = 804 WU) fits any two coins (544 WU)

If you reverse #33223, it still passes, which means it misses the tie-break

### The fix
The test now uses `mixed_weight_pool and adds an extra light coin so that only two light coins can fit together and evicts a coin on every tie to pass.
Lowers the max weight to 536 WU; SRD now has to evict the heavier coin on every tie to succeed

This should show failed tests with [bitcoin#33223](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33223) reverted and pass on master.

pulls.title: mining: avoid checkBlock crash when chain has no tip
pulls.body:
**The problem**: `Init.makeMining` returns as soon as the chainstate is loaded. On a first start with an empty datadir, or on a node started with `-reindex`/`-reindex-chainstate`, this is before the genesis block is connected, so the active chain has no tip. A `Mining.checkBlock` call in this window reaches `TestBlockValidity()`, which asserts that the tip exists, and the node aborts.

**The fix**: in `MakeMining`, if `wait_loaded` is set, wait for the chainstate to be present and for the tip to be non-null. 

*Alternative fix*: In `Mining.checkBlock`, check if the tip is present, return early with "inconclusive-no-chain-tip" otherwise. (I initially implemented this fix, but decided to go with the `makeMining` one instead, see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36908#discussion_r4610682758)

The crash can be reproduced on master using the functional test included in this PR.

This is joint work with Turtlecute33 :)

pulls.title: refactor: extract per-message helpers from ProcessMessage (move-only)
pulls.body:
`PeerManagerImpl::ProcessMessage()` is a ~1500-line function handling every p2p message type inline, which makes it hard to navigate and review.

This PR continues splitting it into per-message helper functions, following the pattern of the recently merged fa5ab0220e02377c3c855042ecdf1f5f950d0965 (`ProcessPong()`) and fa55723b8fbd4fd056dddac5b35daf2e86021422 (`ProcessAddrs()`), as suggested by maflcko https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34588#issuecomment-4658892004.

A preparatory commit removes the `__func__` prefix from one getheaders debug log, so moving it doesn't change the output.

Nine handlers are extracted, one move-only commit each:

  * `ProcessGetAddr()` — `getaddr`
  * `ProcessGetDataMessage()` — `getdata` (named to avoid colliding with the existing `ProcessGetData()`, which services the request queue this handler fills)
  * `ProcessGetBlocks()` — `getblocks`
  * `ProcessGetHeaders()` — `getheaders`
  * `ProcessInv()` — `inv`
  * `ProcessSendTxRcncl()` — `sendtxrcncl`
  * `ProcessTx()` — `tx`
  * `ProcessCompactBlock()` — `cmpctblock`
  * `ProcessVersion()` — `version`

Each extraction commit is a code move with indentation adjustments: the only new lines are the declaration (with thread-safety annotations), the function signature, and the one-line call site.
Each call site is `Helper(...); return;`, so `return` statements inside the moved bodies keep identical semantics. No behavior change beyond debug log output.

One final cleanup commit normalizes the remaining formatting, replaces equivalent `break` statements with `return` in `ProcessSendTxRcncl()`, and simplifies the `send_getaddr` conditional in `ProcessVersion()`.

Each extraction commit can be reviewed with the git options:
`--color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=ignore-all-space`

Declarations and definitions are placed next to related existing helpers (e.g. `ProcessGetDataMessage` next to `ProcessGetData`, `ProcessGetBlocks` next to `ProcessGetBlockData`, `ProcessGetAddr` after `ProcessAddrs`).

pulls.title: validation: check the most recent AssumeUTXO commitment during IBD
pulls.body:
**Problem:** AssumeUTXO verifies imported UTXOs against a hash we bake into the binary.
Every node reconstructs the same UTXO set during ordinary IBD, but [does not check its hash against the existing AssumeUTXO commitment](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/32377).

**Fix:** During ordinary block validation, verify the AssumeUTXO hash when block connection reaches the corresponding block.
Log mismatches and raise a GUI/RPC warning while allowing IBD to continue.
Flush pending changes to disk before hashing the UTXO set and comparing the result with the commitment.

Keep only the latest AssumeUTXO commitment per network to limit the extra hashing work during IBD, and update the release process to replace it.
Users who need older snapshots for research or other purposes can use a compatible older release or restore the corresponding commitment as `m_assumeutxo_data` and recompile.

pulls.title: cmake: De-duplicate libraries where possible
pulls.body:
Set the [CMP0156](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/policy/CMP0156.html) and [CMP0179](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/policy/CMP0179.html) policies to NEW. CMP0156 de-duplicates libraries on link lines based on linker capabilities; CMP0179 makes this de-duplication keep the first occurrence of static libraries. This silences Apple linker "ignoring duplicate libraries" warnings.

Both policies are gated on CMP0179, which requires CMake >=3.31, to avoid the intermediate CMake 3.29/3.30 behaviour where only CMP0156 is available. This requirement is satisfied by the current Homebrew package and the Guix build environment. On older versions, the policy guard makes this a no-op.

The Guix scripts for macOS have been updated to turn linker warnings into errors, as is [done](https://github.com/fanquake/bitcoin/commit/1714953eff0544d6085c4c1cc4270a891dd995c0) for other targets.

pulls.title: util: Add and use AssertUnreachable
pulls.body:
The current code uses assertions with falsy literal values in a few places. This is perfectly fine, but this comes with a bit of confusion sometimes:

* `assert(false)` may cause confusion when it is unclear if `NDEBUG` can disable it. (The intention is to disallow `NDEBUG` compilation). Also, it can lead to warnings when used with clang-cl.exe (GCC seems to understand it)
* `Assert(false)` hides the noreturn attribute behind a function call, which may cause GCC return-type warnings. (Clang seems to understand it)

See https://godbolt.org/z/h7PT3jh3Y for the clang-cl/GCC warning reproducer.

* When C++23 will be allowed, devs may prefer `std::unreachable`. However, this is unsafe and will invoke UB.
* There is confusion why a `CHECK_NONFATAL` macro exists, but no fatal equivalent.

Fix all those issues by:

* Adding a new `AssertUnreachable`, which directly calls the noreturn `internal_abort_helper` helper.
* Adding an `assert_falsy` linter to enforce code to use this macro.

pulls.title: qa: assert_equals -> assert_true/assert_false
pulls.body:
Instead of this in the functional tests:
```python
    assert_equals([long expression pushing next arg to the right], True)
    assert_equals([other long expression pushing next arg to the right], False)
```
we get:
```python
    assert_true([long expression without arg on the right side..])
    assert_false([other long expression without next arg to the right.])
```

The main point of this change is that `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` reduce cognitive tokens when scanning the code (equals to *what*...?). (As a consequence, `assert_true()`/`assert_false()` are also common in other test frameworks).

`assert_equals()` continues to be used in cases where we don't compare to boolean literals.

`assert_true([expression])` is different from plain `assert [expression]` in that `assert` is truthy while `assert_true` requires boolean `True`. (`assert` can also be deactivated when executing Python code in optimized mode (see https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/30529#discussion_r1893029530)).

A smaller scale attempt at introducing `assert_true()` was originally included in #31874 before being dropped.

pulls.title: scripted-diff: Type-safe settings retrieval
pulls.body:
This PR changes the way settings are registered and retrieved to provide more compile-time safety. Currently settings are [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L504) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/03cff2c1421e5db59963eba1a845ef5dd318c275/src/init.cpp#L173) like:

```c++
// Register setting
argsman.AddArg("-pid=<file>", strprintf("Specify pid file. Relative paths will be prefixed by a net-specific datadir location. (default: %s)", BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME), ArgsManager::ALLOW_ANY, OptionsCategory::OPTIONS);

// Retrieve setting
args.GetPathArg("-pid", BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME)
```

But this is not ideal because nothing checks that setting names are spelled correctly, or that default values (`BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME`) are used consistently in the help string and retrieval sites, or that settings are retrieved with consistent types (bool, int, string, path, or list). This PR addresses these issues by adding setting [declarations](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init_settings.h#L267-L270) which allow settings to be [registered](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L484) and [retrieved](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/416860fc360b3d5aa1a0782ab8f8454b46e6d657/src/init.cpp#L164C38-L164C59) like:

```c++
// Declare setting
using PidSetting = common::Setting<
    "-pid=<file>", fs::path, {.legacy = true},
    "Specify pid file. Relative paths will be prefixed by a net-specific datadir location. (default: %s)">
    ::DefaultFn<[] { return BITCOIN_PID_FILENAME; }>;

// Register setting
PidSetting::Register(argsman);

// Retrieve setting
PidSetting::Get(args)
```

---

#### Suggestions for review

All the real changes in this PR are in the last scripted-diff commit:

- [scripted-diff: Replace AddArgs / GetArgs calls with Setting Register / Get calls](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/73c1f852eba2a48be0f03816a957e46ce6275bd9)

If you take a few minutes to look at the changes applied in this scripted-diff commit, you'll understand everything this PR is doing. A good place to start looking around in this commit is the generated [`src/init_settings.h`](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init_settings.h) file which declares the settings that get registered in [src/init.cpp](https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/blob/pr/scripty/src/init.cpp). Then you can look at the surrounding diffs and see they are just replacing `AddArg` and `GetArg` calls.

The other notable commit is second commit, which implements the `Setting` class:

- [common: Add Setting class to support typed Settings](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31260/commits/9c1cdb31eac5a180950dee0c6135918ce70b60f1)

The other commits do minor things like moving code or updating linters. The python script that implements the scripted diff is a temporary artifact that gets deleted. The python script is complicated because it does things like parsing c++ code to extract help strings, and figuring out the right types to declare settings with so code compiles. But the entire scope of the script is to (1) generate Setting type definitions, (2) add #includes, and (3) replace `AddArg()` calls with `Register()` calls and `GetArg()` calls with `Get()` calls. So there is not much the script can actually do wrong without triggering build and test failures.

---

#### Extensions

This PR only adds the ability to declare individual settings with built-in types. It doesn't provide any new runtime behavior, but a branch in issue #22978 extends the `Setting` class implemented here to support runtime setting validation, additional types like `std::variant`, additional conversion options, custom types, custom validation, and groups of settings declared as options structs.

This change is mostly orthogonal to #16545. #16545 only provides runtime type checking while this PR only provides compile-time checking with no new runtime behavior. But this change does allow a nicer way of declaring types in #16545, using c++ types like `int` instead of flags like `ALLOW_INT`, or`std::vector<std::string>` instead of `ALLOW_STRING | ALLOW_LIST`.

pulls.title: wallet: Fix ScanForWalletTransactions missing tx when look-ahead pool expands mid-block
pulls.body:
When `ScanForWalletTransactions` processes a block containing both a transaction to a key just outside the look-ahead pool and a pool-expanding transaction that triggers `TopUp`, and the former appears first in vtx order, the wallet misses the earlier transaction — leaving the balance wrong with no indication a second scan is needed. The fix retries any transaction that doesn't match on a full pass, dropping it once it does, until a pass resolves nothing new — so a transaction can be recognized once something else in the block makes it relevant, regardless of why. The first commit demonstrates the incorrect behaviour; the second contains the fix; the third adds a benchmark guarding the fix's performance on a large, mostly-foreign block with an embedded multi-level cascade.
Bug details...
`ScanForWalletTransactions` iterates over a block's transactions in the order the miner placed them (vtx order). A descriptor wallet maintains a look-ahead pool of pre-derived keys so it can recognise incoming payments. When a payment arrives at a key near the pool boundary, `MarkUnusedAddresses` → `TopUp` extends the pool. If within a single block: - **Tx_lookahead** pays to key index `N` (just outside the current pool `[0, N-1]`), AND - **Tx_expand** pays to key index `N-1` (last in pool — triggers TopUp, extending pool to `[0, 2N-1]`) and Tx_lookahead appears at an earlier vtx position than Tx_expand, the scan misses Tx_lookahead: 1. Tx_lookahead processed: pool = `[0, N-1]` → `IsMine` returns false → missed 2. Tx_expand processed: key `N-1` found → TopUp fires → pool = `[0, 2N-1]` `FastWalletRescanFilter::UpdateIfNeeded()` fires only at the **start of the next block** iteration — there is no mechanism to re-examine Tx_lookahead within the same scan pass. The transaction is not permanently lost — because Tx_expand extended the pool as a side effect, a second explicit `rescanblockchain` call recovers Tx_lookahead. But the wallet shows a wrong balance with no indication a second scan is needed. This bug does not affect live `blockConnected` when both transactions pass through the mempool first: `transactionAddedToMempool(Tx_expand)` pre-extends the pool before the block arrives, so vtx ordering does not matter. It only manifests in `ScanForWalletTransactions` (rescan paths) for descriptor wallets.
Affected callers...
**Callers affected** (all use `ScanForWalletTransactions`): - `rescanblockchain` - `importdescriptors` (via `RescanFromTime`) - `restorewallet` and wallet migration watchonly/solvable wallets (via `AttachChain`)
Fix details and performance...
**Fix:** during the per-block vtx loop, keep a list of still-unmatched vtx positions. Retry it each pass, dropping positions once `SyncTransaction()` returns `true` for them, until a full pass resolves nothing new. A transaction becomes resolvable once something else earlier in the same block changes its relevance — either a pool expansion (`TopUp` from `MarkUnusedAddresses`) now covering a key it pays, or a previously-unknown parent transaction becoming known so a spend of it is recognized. The unmatched set never grows, so this terminates without a safety cap. This also covers two cases a shrinking-prefix rescan (an earlier version of this fix) did not: a prefix-recovered receive that triggers a second pool expansion past where the prefix had already shrunk to (see Part 5), and a same-block spend of a look-ahead receive only recognized later in the same pass via a parent-tx lookup rather than a pool expansion (see Part 6, molnard's finding — see Notes below). **Performance:** the retry loop costs at most one extra pass for any block containing a wallet-relevant transaction during a rescan, in typical shapes. The worst case is a large, mostly-foreign block with a multi-level cascade embedded in it. `bench_bitcoin -filter=RescanCascadeInLargeBlock` guards that scenario against regression.
Test coverage...
**Regression test:** `test/functional/wallet_rescan_intrablock_ordering.py` - Part 1: loadwallet rescan — Tx_lookahead found after fix. - Part 2: importdescriptors full rescan from genesis — Tx_lookahead found after fix. - Part 3: second rescanblockchain recovers Tx_lookahead (pre-fix behaviour, kept as sanity check). - Part 4: two-level cascade — two successive TopUp events fire in one block, both lookahead txs found, validating the bounded multi-pass loop. - Part 5: a prefix-recovered receive triggers a second TopUp past where a shrinking-prefix rescan would have already stopped. - Part 6: a same-block spend of a look-ahead receive only recognized later in the same pass (molnard's finding).
Manual reproduction (regtest) ```bash bitcoind -regtest -keypool=5 -fallbackfee=0.0001 -daemon bitcoin-cli -regtest -named createwallet wallet_name=funding bitcoin-cli -regtest generatetoaddress 102 $(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding getnewaddress) bitcoin-cli -regtest -named createwallet wallet_name=test RECV_DESC=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listdescriptors \ | jq -r '[.descriptors[] | select(.internal==false and .range!=null)][0].desc') END_RANGE=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listdescriptors \ | jq '[.descriptors[] | select(.internal==false and .range!=null)][0].range[1]') ADDR_EXPAND=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest deriveaddresses "$RECV_DESC" "[$END_RANGE,$END_RANGE]" | jq -r '.[0]') ADDR_LOOKAHEAD=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest deriveaddresses "$RECV_DESC" "[$((END_RANGE+1)),$((END_RANGE+1))]" | jq -r '.[0]') bitcoin-cli -regtest unloadwallet test TXID1=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding sendtoaddress "$ADDR_LOOKAHEAD" 0.001) TXID2=$(bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=funding sendtoaddress "$ADDR_EXPAND" 0.001) bitcoin-cli -regtest generateblock "raw(51)" "[\"$TXID1\",\"$TXID2\"]" # First scan — TXID1 missing, wrong balance bitcoin-cli -regtest loadwallet test bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions # Second scan — TXID1 recovered bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test rescanblockchain bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions # With the fix (this PR's tip), both transactions are found on the first scan. bitcoin-cli -regtest loadwallet test bitcoin-cli -regtest -rpcwallet=test listtransactions ```
_**Notes**_: * Originally noted by furszy in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/31629#issuecomment-2657775368; his "case 2" describes a related but harder inter-block variant: new blocks arriving via `blockConnected` during an active rescan with a not-yet-expanded pool. That problem remains a potential follow-up. This PR fixes the simpler intra-block sub-case where the miss happens entirely within a single block's vtx loop, with no concurrent block arrivals required. * Perhaps the issue is related to the symptom was previously reported in #19808 but could not be reproduced at the time and was closed without a fix. * molnard [found](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35901#pullrequestreview-5041935034) a related gap the shrinking-prefix rescan didn't close: if a parent tx pays a look-ahead key and a later tx in the same block spends that parent's output, and the spend sits at or after the block's last pool expansion, the prefix rescan recovers the parent but never revisits the spend. jeanpablojp separately found a second gap in the same shrinking-prefix approach — a prefix-recovered receive that triggers a further pool expansion past where the prefix had already shrunk to (Part 5) — and proposed and benchmarked the fix now in this PR: retry based on each tx's `SyncTransaction()` result until a full pass causes no change, rather than tracking a shrinking prefix. Both gaps are now fixed in this PR (Parts 5 and 6).
